opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't one moment. It was more a pattern I kept noticing in how Ege approached problems.

When we started Epoch, much of our work was empirical: tracking compute, data, and algorithmic progress, and trying to get clean trend lines. Ege was strong at that, but what stood out was that he always wanted to ask the next question. Okay, compute is growing this fast, but what does that actually *imply*? What happens to output, to wages, to the growth rate of the economy if these systems can substitute for human labor? He'd go straight to the underlying model rather than stopping at the chart.

He also has an unusual combination of mathematical fluency and a willingness to take economic theory seriously without being captured by its conventions. Many people in AI wave their hands at the economics, saying "it'll be transformative," without engaging with the growth literature, the production functions, or why historical growth looked the way it did. And many economists dismiss explosive growth scenarios because they look so far outside the historical data. Ege was comfortable in both worlds. He'd read the semi-endogenous growth papers, find the assumptions that actually drive the conclusions, and then ask whether those assumptions survive once you can scale AI the way you scale capital.

He was also just very good at arguing. We'd disagree, he'd write a quick model to make his point precise, and half the time I'd come out having changed my mind. That's what you want in someone working on questions where the conventional wisdom might be badly wrong. So it felt natural that the economic side, meaning what AI does to growth, labor, and the broader economy, was where he could have the most leverage.

r001.rationale: The response describes Ege’s engagement with economic theory, but does not say Tamay found him more knowledgeable about economics than almost any of his Cambridge peers.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't so much that I convinced Ege as that I noticed what he was already doing. When I first encountered him, he had this unusual combination: he was very strong in mathematics, he had a deep interest in history, and he kept gravitating toward questions about long-run growth almost on his own. He'd show up having read Kremer, or the old Romer papers, or some obscure piece on the industrial revolution, and he'd have opinions about where the models went wrong.

What struck me was that most people who are good at the technical side of AI don't really think seriously about the economics, and most economists don't really take seriously the possibility of a true discontinuity in the production of ideas. Ege was comfortable in both worlds. He could read a growth model and immediately ask whether its assumptions about the substitutability of labor and capital still held if you could just run more copies of a researcher.

So the pitch I made to him was pretty simple: these are some of the most important questions you could work on, almost nobody is working on them with the right tools, and we have the data and the latitude to do it properly. At Epoch we were already tracking compute, algorithmic progress, and training runs, and the natural next question is, what does all of that actually imply for the economy? How fast could output grow, what are the bottlenecks, what happens to wages and interest rates if AI really does what the trend lines suggest it might?

And the other thing is that Ege is fundamentally honest about uncertainty. He'd rather say "the models disagree and here's why" than pick a dramatic number for effect. That matters a lot when the topic invites hype in both directions. So it was less a sales job and more recognizing that he was the right person and just making sure he had the room to do it.

r001.rationale: The response describes Ege’s interest in economic questions and his ability to engage with growth models, but it does not say Tamay considered him more knowledgeable about economics than almost any of his peers at Cambridge.

astra-6.text:
The key thing is that the questions we’re trying to answer at Epoch aren’t just technical questions about AI. They’re also economic questions: how much people will invest in training, what constraints they’ll run into, and how improvements in capabilities translate into economic value.

So the case for Ege working on economics is that you want someone who can connect those pieces—someone who can take an apparently complicated question, identify the assumptions that actually matter, and work through their implications. That kind of reasoning is especially valuable when you’re trying to understand something where we don’t yet have much direct evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says Ege can connect technical and economic questions, but does not state that Tamay considered him more knowledgeable about economics than almost any of his Cambridge peers.

sol-6.1.text: What stood out about Ege was how good he was at reasoning through unfamiliar problems. You could pose an economic question to him, and he’d quickly identify the assumptions that mattered and work out their implications. That seemed especially valuable at Epoch, where many of the questions we care about don’t fit neatly into an existing literature. I thought he could help us make progress on them.
